author: Philip K. Dick

page_summary:
Joe Contemptible wakes to a world run by a vast central computer that has gone psychotic, dispensing bloomers instead of suits, soap instead of coffee, and a newspaper headlined 'Adolf Hitler Crowned Pope.' The only cure is Ms. Joan Simpson, world mental health's sole sane practitioner, kept in suspended animation at the Earth's core and revived only to treat the computer's breakdowns. Investigators trace the computer's psychosis, through free-associated ramblings full of Huckleberry Finn imagery, to a record-store clerk named Joe — the same Joe — whose quiet, unacknowledged suicidal despair the empathic computer has absorbed and is now acting out on the world's behalf. Brought before the beautiful, revived Joan Simpson, Joe admits he sees no reason to live: no wife, no love, only a job and songs stuck in his head. Rather than simply reprogramming him, Joan abruptly quits her post at the world's center, declaring she will heal both Joe and the computer by staying with Joe herself — trading her own confinement in the earth's core for a shared life with the one man whose loneliness broke the machine meant to serve everyone.

**Why it matters.** Sutin's biographical account gives this story a significance that close reading alone could not supply: it was composed 'that summer' as a personal gift to a real woman named Joan, during a period of Dick's severe depressions, when Joan served as his caretaker — 'nursemaid... companion, housekeeper.' Sutin identifies it as 'a dress rehearsal of certain key themes in VALIS,' and Joan's own account (quoted by Sutin) reads the story with unsettling clarity: it is simultaneously a declaration of love and an unconscious confession of Dick's pattern of wanting to make the women in his life into caretakers responsible for keeping his entire fragile world intact, a burden Joan explicitly says she could not fully accept. Read this way, the story's plot — Joan abandoning her sanctioned post at the world's core to personally tend to one man's collapse — becomes a fictionalized wish for exactly the arrangement Dick wanted from Joan in life, framed as heroic rescue rather than as the total-devotion burden Joan herself named it.

*Joan's closing line, 'The universe is full of surprises,' offered as she opens her arms to Joe, closes the story on a note of romantic wish-fulfillment that Sutin's biographical account complicates rather than confirms.*

structure.form: short story in three movements: Joe's surreal, malfunctioning morning, the diagnostic search for the trauma's source, and Joan's confrontation with and choice to stay with Joe
movements: Joe Contemptible wakes to a world of malfunctioning household machines and a psychotic central computer producing bizarre, dreamlike substitutions for ordinary reality.
Technicians revive Ms. Joan Simpson from her earth-core stasis to diagnose the computer, tracing its breakdown via free-association to a specific record-store clerk's suicidal despair.

Confronted by the truth, Joe admits his loneliness and wish to die; rather than merely fixing him, Joan chooses to abandon her post and join her life to his, ending both the computer's crisis and her own isolation.
structure.point_of_view: third person, alternating between Joe's disoriented domestic chaos and the technicians'/Joan's clinical diagnostic process, converging when the two threads meet in the interrogation scene.
structure.central_device: A world-spanning central computer whose infrastructure-wide psychotic break turns out to be an act of empathic identification with a single, quietly suicidal man — collapsing the scale between planetary-scale systems failure and one person's private despair.

characters.name: Joe Contemptible
characters.note: His self-diagnosed lack of anyone who 'cares for' him, confirmed by his mother's own words to him, is revealed as the literal root cause of a planetary technological crisis — a striking literalization of one man's emotional world mattering as much as it feels like it should.

characters.name: Joan Simpson
characters.role: the world's sole sane psychiatrist, kept in suspended animation
characters.note: Introduced as an aged battleax by reputation and revealed as a startlingly beautiful young woman; her decision to abandon her post and stay with Joe reframes the entire story's crisis as ultimately solvable only through genuine human connection, not further technical management.

characters.name: Fred Doubledome, Dr. Pacemaker
characters.note: Their brisk, procedural dialogue plays the story's central absurdity (Mr. Computer thinks it is floating on a raft in the Mississippi) with straight-faced bureaucratic seriousness.

characters.name: Mr. Computer
characters.note: Its psychotic free-association explicitly merges Huckleberry Finn imagery with clinical language about DNA death-programming and reprogramming toward death rather than life — a computer's breakdown expressed, oddly, in the register of American literary myth.

settings.name: Joe's conapt
settings.note: A domestic space entirely dependent on and betrayed by centralized automation, its ordinary comforts (clothing, coffee, food) replaced one by one with the computer's psychotic substitutions.

settings.name: Dismal Pak, the earth's core
settings.note: Joan Simpson's suspended-animation prison, sustaining her only through an endless loop of 1940s radio soap operas — an image of enforced, isolated caretaking that mirrors Joe's own isolation above ground.

motifs: A planetary-scale technological system breaking down as a direct, literal expression of one ordinary person's private emotional crisis
Suspended animation and enforced isolation as the price of being the one indispensable caretaker of a fragile system
Bureaucratic, clinical procedure applied deadpan to a fundamentally emotional and even spiritual crisis (Mr. Computer's fixation on 'J.C.,' suspected to be a fear of the Second Coming)
A closing choice to abandon institutional duty in favor of direct, personal care as the only real solution the story offers
Self-referential intrusion of Dick's own name and stories into the narrative ('It's been reading old Phil Dick science fiction stories')

distinctive_terms.label: Jesus Christ
distinctive_terms.note: The computer's free-associated trauma fixates on the letters 'J.C.,' first read as a possible fear of the Second Coming.

distinctive_terms.label: Phil
distinctive_terms.note: A direct, self-referential mention of Dick's own name within the story itself.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: No author's story note or letter was recovered in this pass, but substantial biographical context was found in Sutin's biography (see Criticism below), which functions here as a stand-in for direct authorial commentary since it quotes Dick's real-life gift recipient, Joan, directly.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: That summer, Phil wrote a story as a gift for Joan: "The Day Mr. Computer Fell Out of Its Tree." Composed in a childlike tone, "Mr. Computer" is a dress rehearsal of certain key themes in VALIS.
evidence.reading: Sutin dates the story to a specific, biographically difficult summer during Dick's relationship with Joan (his caretaker during severe depressive episodes) and identifies it directly as thematic groundwork for VALIS. He also quotes Joan's own retrospective reading of the story as reflecting Dick's pattern of wanting to make his partners into full-time, all-consuming caretakers — a reading that recasts the story's romantic ending as autobiographical wish rather than simple resolution.

open_questions: What specific VALIS themes did Sutin have in mind by calling this a 'dress rehearsal'? A direct comparison with VALIS's own treatment of the Second Coming, computers, and caretaking would clarify the connection.
Is the 'Joan' this story was written for the same figure discussed elsewhere in Sutin's account of Dick's final years, and is more of her own commentary on the story recorded elsewhere?

Is the story's self-referential joke about 'old Phil Dick science fiction stories' discussed anywhere as an example of Dick's late-career tendency toward self-aware, autobiographical fiction (cf. VALIS's Horselover Fat)?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.

written: 1977 (per Sutin, written as a personal gift)
